title: Likes, dislikes, and free time
title_target: ມັກຫຍັງ — Mak nyǎng
goal: Say what you like and dislike at different strengths, talk about your weekends, and turn down an offer without giving offense — all with one verb that never changes form.

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — Planning the weekend
dialogs.intro: Bounmy and Budi swap stories about their free time. Notice how the degree of liking goes up and down without the verb itself changing at all.

notes: **ມັກ mak = "like", and its strength is set by the words around it, not by its form.** From strongest to weakest: *ມັກຫຼາຍທີ່ສຸດ* (like most) → *ມັກຫຼາຍ* (like a lot) → *ມັກ* (like) → *ບໍ່ຄ່ອຍມັກ* (not really like) → *ບໍ່ມັກ* (don't like) → *ບໍ່ມັກເລີຍ* (don't like at all).
**ບໍ່ຄ່ອຍມັກ bàw khàwy mak is the polite way to say no**, and it is often what "don't like" really means. Saying *ບໍ່ມັກເລີຍ* sounds harsh — save it for things you truly hate.

**ມ່ວນ mùan = "fun, enjoyable", and it is a very Lao word.** It is used for experiences, not objects: *ມ່ວນຫຼາຍ* (so much fun), *ບໍ່ມ່ວນ* (no fun). The Thai equivalent is *สนุก*, but *ມ່ວນ* feels warmer and more intimate.

**ຫຼິ້ນ lîn = "play", and it attaches to many leisure activities.** *ຫຼິ້ນກິລາ* (play sports), *ຫຼິ້ນດົນຕີ* (play music), *ໄປຫຼິ້ນ* (go out, hang out), *ຍ່າງຫຼິ້ນ* (take a stroll). If someone invites you to *ໄປຫຼິ້ນ*, it is a casual outing with no particular goal.

**Two words for "can": ໄດ້ dâi and ເປັນ pen.** *ໄດ້* means "be able to, be allowed to, have the chance to" — *ໄປໄດ້* (can go). *ເປັນ* means "can because you have learned how" — *ຮ້ອງເພງເປັນ* (can sing), *ລອຍນ້ຳເປັນ* (can swim), *ຂັບລົດເປັນ* (can drive). ⚠️ Mixing these two up is the mistake people notice fastest.

**ກວ່າ kwàa = "more…than", and ທີ່ສຸດ thìi-sút = "most".** *ດີກວ່າ* (better), *ດີທີ່ສຸດ* (best). To name what you are comparing with, put it after *ກວ່າ*: *ອັນນີ້ດີກວ່າອັນນັ້ນ* (this one is better than that one).

**ເລີຍ lóei after a negative sentence means "at all".** *ບໍ່ມັກເລີຍ* (don't like it at all), *ບໍ່ຮູ້ເລີຍ* (have no idea at all), *ບໍ່ມີເລີຍ* (there's none at all). This is a different use of *ເລີຍ* from "straight away" in unit 3 — the negative context is what marks it.
**ໂອຍ ôoy is an exclamation that softens a refusal.** Like "oh dear" or "oof" in English, it signals that what comes next is not good news — and that alone keeps your refusal from sounding abrupt.
**Karaoke is the number-one social activity in Laos.** It's fine to say no, but know that the invitation is sincere, not just politeness. Go once and sing however badly, and you will make friends.

after: **ກໍໄດ້ *kaw dâi*** is the most useful answer in Laos: "sure, whatever, anything works". Asked what you want to eat, the answer *ຫຍັງກໍໄດ້ nyǎng kaw dâi* (anything is fine) is always safe and always sounds friendly.

blocks.text: To state a hobby, just put *ມັກ* in front of it: *ຂ້ອຍມັກເບິ່ງໜັງ* (I like watching movies). The verb itself doesn't change form at all — no "-ing" needed.

blocks.text: **ແລ້ວແຕ່ເຈົ້າ *lèeo tèe jâo*** (up to you) is a very common answer that foreigners easily misread. It is not a sign of indifference — in Lao culture, handing the choice to someone else is a form of courtesy. If you're on the receiving end, make the decision; that's what is expected.
